explanations.explanation: Joshua, Israel's leader, gets a full-roster order this time: “Take the whole army with you, and go up and attack Ai.” Last time it was only about three thousand men (Joshua 7:4). That's the difference between moving a couch with one friend and moving it with the whole group chat. Everybody shows up.

Close, friend, but that's the number from the first try. About three thousand of Israel's men went up against Ai and fled (Joshua 7:4). This time Joshua, Israel's leader, hears something different: “Take the whole army with you…” Pressing the same blurry stamp twice and expecting a sharp cookie is a mistake I made for years.

The elders do show up, but not alone. Joshua, Israel's leader, is told to take the whole army. Later the elders of Israel march in front of the troops with him (Joshua 8:10), so the troops are right behind them. An army of only elders would be one very slow parade.

That's right. The LORD says to do to Ai and its king as was done to Jericho and its king, "except that you may carry off their plunder and livestock for yourselves." That's a change from Jericho. I think that's a pretty big deal for the people carrying the load.

Look at the second half of the verse. The LORD says, "And you shall do to Ai and its king as you did to Jericho and its king, except that you may carry off their plunder and livestock for yourselves." So the plunder and livestock are allowed this time. That's the one exception.

explanations.answer: Set up an ambush behind the city
explanations.explanation: Yes, the LORD says, "Set up an ambush behind the city." Nobody has to storm the front gate and hope for the best. The plan gets Ai out of the front door while some of Israel's men wait behind it. It's patient work, like waiting for the timer instead of opening the oven every thirty seconds.

explanations.answer: March around the city seven times
explanations.explanation: That's Jericho's plan, not Ai's. At Jericho the people marched around the city once a day for six days, and on the seventh day they went around it seven times (Joshua 6:15). Ai gets a different plan. The LORD tells Joshua, "Set up an ambush behind the city."

explanations.answer: Wait for the city to surrender
explanations.explanation: The LORD never mentions waiting for a surrender. He gives Joshua an action plan: "Set up an ambush behind the city." Nobody is told to sit and hope Ai changes its mind. Waiting around for good news is what I did in that drawer, and it took a long time.
Yes. Joshua says that when Ai comes out against them, "we will flee from them." That's the plan, not a panic. The running is the bait that pulls Ai away from its city.
No surrendering in this plan. Joshua says, "we will flee from them." Running away on purpose is very different from giving up. One is a plan, and the other is just a very short battle.
Joshua never talks about offering peace here. He says, "we will flee from them." The running is what draws Ai away from the city. Handing out peace offers would have spoiled the whole trick.

explanations.answer: They'll think Israel is running like before
explanations.explanation: That's what Joshua says: "The Israelites are running away from us as they did before." Ai is expecting a repeat, so they're ready to see one. Joshua is counting on them seeing exactly what they expect. It works the same way as telling yourself "I'll just have one cookie."

explanations.answer: They'll think Israel is out of supplies
explanations.explanation: Supplies never come up. Joshua says what Ai will say: "The Israelites are running away from us as they did before." It's about the memory of the first battle, not about the camp's pantry. Ai thinks it's seeing a repeat.

explanations.answer: They'll think Joshua has been hurt
explanations.explanation: The text says nothing about Joshua being hurt. What Ai will say is, "The Israelites are running away from us as they did before." So Ai is looking at a repeat of the first battle. Joshua is fine, and he's the one leading the whole thing.

That's right. Joshua tells the men in ambush, "you are to rise from the ambush and seize the city." The signal is Israel fleeing and Ai chasing. He adds, "for the LORD your God will deliver it into your hand." Good timing is half of any plan.

The ambush does move, and Joshua says when. As Israel flees, "you are to rise from the ambush and seize the city." It's True, because the men don't stay put forever. He adds that "the LORD your God will deliver it into your hand."
Yes. Joshua says, "set it on fire." That's the order once the ambush has taken the city. Later the smoke rising is what Ai sees when they look back (Joshua 8:20).
Not rebuild. The order is, "set it on fire." By the end, Joshua has made Ai "a permanent heap of ruins" (Joshua 8:28). Nobody is picking up a hammer here.
No searching in the orders. Joshua says, "set it on fire." That's the instruction for after the city is taken. The fire turns out to be the signal that Ai sees from far away.
Not quite, friend. Joshua doesn't stay behind. The text says he "and the elders of Israel marched before them up to Ai." So Joshua is at the front, and the elders walk with him.
That's right. Joshua got up early and mobilized his men, and "he and the elders of Israel marched before them up to Ai." He goes in front, not behind. The troops follow him.

Yes, north. The troops "camped to the north of it, with the valley between them and the city." The ambush is on the other side, to the west. So Ai has Israel in front of it and has no idea who is behind it.
Not south. The troops camped "to the north of it, with the valley between them and the city." The ambush sits to the west, between Bethel and Ai. South doesn't come up.
East isn't it. The troops camped "to the north of it, with the valley between them and the city." Joshua's hidden men are to the west, between Bethel and Ai. Both groups are placed on purpose.

Not quite. The text says the king of Ai "did not know that an ambush had been set up against him behind the city." He is focused on the army he can see. It's a bit like watching the counter while the oven timer goes off behind you.

That's right. The king of Ai hurries out early in the morning, but "he did not know that an ambush had been set up against him behind the city." He sees one army and doesn't know about the other. That's why the plan works.
Yes. Joshua and all Israel "fled toward the wilderness." They let themselves be beaten back, and Ai follows. That pulls the men of Ai away from their city.
The Jordan is where Israel crossed into the land (Joshua 3), but it isn't where they run here. They "fled toward the wilderness." That's how Ai gets pulled away from its city.
Jericho is the city Israel already took (Joshua 6), but they don't run there. The text says they "fled toward the wilderness." The men of Ai follow them in that direction.
Not true. The text says "Not a man was left in Ai or Bethel who did not go out after Israel." Nobody stayed to watch the city. It's "wide open" while they chase.

That's right. "Not a man was left in Ai or Bethel who did not go out after Israel, leaving the city wide open while they pursued Israel." No guards, no watchmen. Everyone goes out, and the city is left behind them.
Yes. The LORD says, "Hold out your battle lance toward Ai, for into your hand I will deliver the city." Joshua holds it out, and the men in ambush rise as soon as he does. It works as the signal.

A staff shows up in other places. Moses, Israel's earlier leader, was told to lift his staff over the sea (Exodus 14:16). Here the LORD says, "Hold out your battle lance toward Ai." That's what Joshua holds out.

Trumpets belong to Jericho, where seven priests carried seven trumpets of rams' horns (Joshua 6:4). At Ai the LORD says, "Hold out your battle lance toward Ai." Joshua does, and the ambush moves as soon as he does.
Yes, smoke. "The smoke of the city was rising into the sky." The men of Ai turn around and see it. That's the moment they learn their city has been taken.
Dust would be a good guess for a chase, but that's not what the text says. It says "the smoke of the city was rising into the sky." The ambush set the city on fire, and the men of Ai see it.
Not mist. It says "the smoke of the city was rising into the sky." The men of Ai turn around and see it. It's the first sign that the city has been taken.
Not true. The text says, "They could not escape in any direction." The city behind them is burning, and Israel's troops turn on them from the other side. There is no open way out.
That's right. "They could not escape in any direction." The city is burning, and the troops who fled to the wilderness turn against their pursuers. The way out is closed in every direction.

explanations.answer: Trapped between Israel on both sides
explanations.explanation: Yes. The men of Ai "were trapped between the Israelite forces on both sides." The ambush came out of the city, and the troops who fled turned around. It's a heavy part of the story, and the text says it plainly.
Not inside the city. The ambush has taken it and set it on fire. The men of Ai "were trapped between the Israelite forces on both sides." It's a heavy moment, and the text says it plainly.

explanations.answer: Scattered toward the hills of Bethel
explanations.explanation: No scattering here. The text says the men of Ai "were trapped between the Israelite forces on both sides." Israel struck them down until no survivor or fugitive remained. It's a heavy part of the story.
Yes. "They took the king of Ai alive and brought him to Joshua." Everyone else in the fight fell, but the king is taken alive. Joshua deals with him later in the passage.

The king of Jericho belongs to the earlier story. The LORD told Joshua to do to Ai and its king as was done to Jericho and its king (Joshua 8:2). Here it's the other king: "they took the king of Ai alive and brought him to Joshua."
Bethel is mentioned as a place, since the ambush lay between Bethel and Ai. The text never mentions a king of Bethel here. It says, "they took the king of Ai alive and brought him to Joshua."

That's right. "Israel took for themselves only the cattle and plunder of that city, as the LORD had commanded Joshua." That's the exception the LORD gave at the start (Joshua 8:2). It's a clean, careful follow-through.

The text says it plainly. "Israel took for themselves only the cattle and plunder of that city, as the LORD had commanded Joshua." The LORD had said at the start that they could carry off the plunder and livestock (Joshua 8:2). So this one is True.
Yes. "Over it they raised a large pile of rocks, which remains to this day." It's a heavy ending for a heavy passage, and the text says it simply. The rocks are still there when the writer tells it.
Not an altar. The text says, "over it they raised a large pile of rocks, which remains to this day." It's a heavy part of the story. A plain heap of stones marks the place.

No pillar here. "Over it they raised a large pile of rocks, which remains to this day." The body was taken down at sunset and thrown at the entrance of the city gate. Rocks cover it, and this is a heavy part of the story.
